original_question: Under the same definitions of Type-A and Type-B vertex orders for a graph G, if G admits a Type-A order or a Type-B order, can such an order be found in polynomial time?
target_in_paper: Section 7, Problem 7.2: "If a Type-A or Type-B order exists, can it be found in polynomial time?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right algorithmic search problem, the right objects (Type-A and Type-B vertex orders of a graph G), the existential premise ('if such an order exists'), and the intended complexity requirement ('in polynomial time'). It is very close to the paper’s official wording in Problem 7.2.
missing_details: The question is not stand-alone because it refers to 'the same definitions' without restating them.
The ambient class should be made explicit: G is a finite simple undirected graph.
One must specify that the sought object is a linear ordering of the vertex set V(G), say v1, ..., vn.
The paper defines d^-(vi) = |{j < i : vivj in E(G)}| and d^+(vi) = |{j > i : vivj in E(G)}| for a chosen linear order; these counts should be included.
Type-A must be stated exactly: for every vertex vi, d^-(vi) is odd or 0.
Type-B must be stated exactly: for every vertex vi, either d^-(vi) is odd or 0, or d^-(vi) is even and d^+(vi) = 0.
It should be explicit that the algorithmic task is to output a witnessing order, not merely to decide existence.

The workshop paper phrases the search question jointly, but the cited source paper separates the two analogous algorithmic problems for the corresponding notions called odd-majority orientations and odd-even orderings.
refined_question: Let G = (V,E) be a finite simple undirected graph. For a linear ordering pi = (v1, ..., vn) of V, define d^-(vi) = |{j < i : vivj in E}| and d^+(vi) = |{j > i : vivj in E}|. Call pi a Type-A order if d^-(vi) is odd or 0 for every i, and call pi a Type-B order if for every i either d^-(vi) is odd or 0, or d^-(vi) is even and d^+(vi) = 0. Given G, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, whenever G admits a Type-A order (respectively, a Type-B order), outputs such a witnessing linear order of V(G)?
justification: The nearest official formulation in arXiv:2411.10046 is exactly Problem 7.2 in Section 7, after the paper introduces Type-A and Type-B orders via the quantities d^- and d^+ attached to a linear vertex order. Your draft is therefore targeting the correct open problem. To make it fully stand-alone, however, the order-dependent definitions must be restated. The cited joint paper of Caro and Tuza is the underlying source of these notions: in Section 3.5 it defines the corresponding parity-constrained vertex-order concepts more formally, explains in Theorem 3.13 why they matter for the anti-Ramsey parameters studied there, and in Section 6.3 records the analogous algorithmic open problems. This confirms that the sharp, paper-faithful refinement is a witness-construction question for these exact order types, not a broader recognition or optimization variant.
